title: "Strategies available for in-house web scraping"

Points to consider if in-house web scraping is the chosen solution\

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Preliminary analysis {#Strategiesavailableforinhousewebscraping-Preliminaryanalysis}

If the National Statistical Office (NSO) decides to perform the web
scraping on its own, some points should be considered to define the best
scraping strategy and the best web scraping tool to adopt or develop.

Once the candidate sites are identified, guidance on web scraping for
Consumer Price Indices (CPIs) (see section 3 of Eurostat\'s \"[Practical
guidelines on web scraping for the
HICP](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/272892/12032198/Guidelines-web-scraping-HICP-11-2020.pdf/)\"
for further discussion) recommends that before putting up any scraping
tools the first strategy to follow is check whether there is an
Application Programming Interface (API) available to extract the desired
data. The use of an API of a given web source allows access to a
structured database that allows the extraction of the source's data with
improved control and stability without the need to scrape. An example on
the use of an API for CPI purposes can be found in Annex II of Ref.
\"[Practical guidelines on web scraping for the
HICP](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/272892/12032198/Guidelines-web-scraping-HICP-11-2020.pdf/)\" and
section \"[Collection of data via
APIs](collection-of-data-via-apis.qmd)\".

Another important issue to consider before scraping a site is to check
what is the site policy regarding web scraping. Some websites have
restrictions against being scraped and may even forbid it. It is a good
practice to follow the site rules. Robots.txt contains the information
about website policies concerning which areas that scrapers are allowed
to search. This file can be accessed by typing the root of the website
and adding \'/robots.txt\'. For instance,
<https://www.ecb.europa.eu/robots.txt>. A more detailed discussion on
legal issues on using web scraping for CPIs is discussed in the
Eurostat\'s \"[Practical guidelines on web scraping for the
HICP](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/272892/12032198/Guidelines-web-scraping-HICP-11-2020.pdf/)\".
Examples of NSOs current practices are presented in Annex VII of this
guidance. The [web scraping policy of the
ONS-UK](https://www.ons.gov.uk/aboutus/transparencyandgovernance/datastrategy/datapolicies/webscrapingpolicy)
is another interesting example on such practices, where permissions to
web scrape are managed centrally to avoid duplication and reduce the
risk of blocking.

# Targeted versus bulk approaches  {#Strategiesavailableforinhousewebscraping-Targetedversusbulkapproaches}

If an API is not available and scraping is allowed, the choice of the
best tool will rely on some factors such as the amount and frequency of
data to be collected from a given site and the number of sites necessary
to provide an appropriate coverage of a given item of the basket.
Regarding these issues, web scraping can be divided in two approaches:
targeted and bulk (\"[Practical guidelines on web scraping for the
HICP](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/272892/12032198/Guidelines-web-scraping-HICP-11-2020.pdf/)\").

Targeted web scraping aims at collecting data whose attributes are
predefined beforehand and hence applies to the collection of a limited
number of items from a given number of websites. This is useful for when
the goal is to [sample from these new data
sources](product-sampling-for-price-index-calculation.qmd) in
order to replace the existing collection, rather than use the full data
set. The bulk approach aims at extracting a large volume of data without
selecting a subset of items to price.

The targeted approach is commonly employed when the goal is to replace
and improve the collection of items of the basket that are usually
performed in a manual centralized approach by means of emails, phone
calls, human inspection of websites, etc. For this kind of problem, it
is desirable to have a more generic web scraping tool that can be used
to extract data from different websites and with a few input and control
parameters that can be defined manually by users. See Ref. (1) and (2)
for some examples.

NSOs have been employing the use of so-called point-and-click
functionality tools to perform targeted extraction of web data. Such
tools are based on user-friendly interfaces where users need to provide
a set of parameters of the sites to extract desired information. There
are third-parties that offer those engines and some NSOs have been
exploring such tools. A disadvantage of using third-party tools is that
they are not designed for the specific needs of CPI collection. For
instance, such services are usually not free of charge and not open
source, hence changes in the underlying scripts according to user needs
are not allowed. For further discussion see section 3 of \"[Practical
guidelines on web scraping for the
HICP](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/272892/12032198/Guidelines-web-scraping-HICP-11-2020.pdf/)\".\

An alternative is to develop fit for purpose tools in-house. A nice
example of such an approach is the RobotTool engine, developed by
Statistics Netherlands for targeted collection of prices. In Ref. (2)
the details for the creation and development of the tool are discussed.
The tool is currently available at
<https://github.com/SNStatComp/RobotTool>, where the license terms are
also presented, although note that as of June 2022, this repo will no
longer be updated to reflect changes on the internal CBS production
version of the tool.

For bulk collection the best option is to scrape by coding since the
manual work to predefine the data of interest would be too resource
intensive. The computational efficiency is also a key point since coded
scrapers will usually run much faster than point and click applications.
The code shall automate the actions that would be conducted by a web
browser such as, opening a webpage, clicking and scrolling, and
selecting the elements of interest by means of a query. Techniques to be
employed will rely on the sites being of a static or dynamic nature
(\"[Practical guidelines on web scraping for the
HICP](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/272892/12032198/Guidelines-web-scraping-HICP-11-2020.pdf/)\").

Due to its free software character, R and Python are popular tools
adopted for web scraping by coding. Also, they already offer dedicated
libraries developed for this goal. Among the most used ones we can cite
[Rvest](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rvest/index.html) and
[RSelenium](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/RSelenium/index.html)
in R, whereas in Python some options available include
[urllib3](https://pypi.org/project/urllib3/),
[BeautifulSoup](https://pypi.org/project/beautifulsoup4/) and
[Scrapy3](https://pypi.org/project/Scrapy3/). The use of Selenium is
necessary whenever the site has a dynamical character which demands the
action of a user interacting with the page in order to get a given
information. Selenium mimics a human in performing such tasks. The
RSelenium library deals with this in R. Selenium is compatible and can
be installed in Python also (see
[here](https://selenium-python.readthedocs.io/installation.html#installing-python-bindings-for-selenium),
for instance). 

In section 3 of \"[Practical guidelines on web scraping for the
HICP](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/documents/272892/12032198/Guidelines-web-scraping-HICP-11-2020.pdf/)\", there
is a detailed discussion on the main software used for coding a scraper
and in Annex VII a list of the tools currently adopted by different
NSOs. A more general discussion on Information Technology (IT)
requirements for these new data sources is available in the section [CPI
production system
requirements](cpi-production-system-requirements.qmd).
